claims.claim: Piezo2 CKO mice exhibit grossly normal skeletal development with no bone fracture.
claims.source: The Piezo2 CKO mice exhibited grossly normal skeletal development with no bone fracture, but the Piezo1/2 double conditional (Piezo1/2 DKO) mutant mice demonstrated more severe skeletal defects including additional fractures in the femur (Figure 2a,b, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by skeletal staining and μCT data shown in Figure 2a,b and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Piezo1/2 DKO mutant mice demonstrate more severe skeletal defects including additional fractures in the femur.
claims.source: The Piezo2 CKO mice exhibited grossly normal skeletal development with no bone fracture, but the Piezo1/2 double conditional (Piezo1/2 DKO) mutant mice demonstrated more severe skeletal defects including additional fractures in the femur (Figure 2a,b, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by skeletal staining and μCT data shown in Figure 2a,b and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Long bones are shortened in the absence of Piezo1.
claims.source: We also found that long bones were shortened in the absence of Piezo1, but not Piezo 2, and further shortening was observed in the Piezo1/2 DKO mutants (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: Supported by μCT measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: Long bones are not shortened in the absence of Piezo2 alone.
claims.source: We also found that long bones were shortened in the absence of Piezo1, but not Piezo 2, and further shortening was observed in the Piezo1/2 DKO mutants (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: Supported by μCT measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: Further shortening of long bones is observed in Piezo1/2 DKO mutants.
claims.source: We also found that long bones were shortened in the absence of Piezo1, but not Piezo 2, and further shortening was observed in the Piezo1/2 DKO mutants (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: Supported by μCT measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: Piezo1 plays a major role while Piezo2 shares some redundant functions with Piezo1 in mesenchymal progenitor cells during skeletal development.
claims.source: These results indicate that while Piezo1 plays a major role, Piezo2 shares some of the Piezo1 functions in mesenchymal progenitor cells during skeletal development.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the differential severity of skeletal phenotypes in Piezo1 CKO, Piezo2 CKO, and Piezo1/2 DKO mice.

claims.claim: Piezo1 expression is progressively increased in young mice postnatally.
claims.source: Mechanical stress increases postnatally and we found that Piezo1 expression was progressively increased in young mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that Piezo1 also regulates bone formation after birth in adult lives.
claims.evidence: Supported by Western blotting and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: Piezo2 mRNA expression is reduced in postnatal mice in the cortical bone.
claims.source: However, Piezo2 mRNA expression was reduced in postnatal mice in the cortical bone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
claims.evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: Both cortical and trabecular bone masses are reduced in Piezo1 CKO mice at P21.
claims.source: The μCT analyses showed that both cortical and trabecular bone masses were reduced in the Piezo1 CKO mice and further reduced in the Piezo1/2 DKO mice at the age of P21.
claims.evidence: Supported by μCT data shown in Figure 2c,d.

claims.claim: Cortical and trabecular bone masses are further reduced in Piezo1/2 DKO mice at P21.
claims.source: The μCT analyses showed that both cortical and trabecular bone masses were reduced in the Piezo1 CKO mice and further reduced in the Piezo1/2 DKO mice at the age of P21.
claims.evidence: Supported by μCT data shown in Figure 2c,d.

claims.claim: Piezo2 CKO mice exhibit normal bone mass at P21.
claims.source: The Piezo2 CKO mice exhibited normal bone mass (Figure 2c,d, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by μCT data shown in Figure 2c,d.

claims.claim: Reduction of collagens in trabecular and cortical bones is observed in P5 Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant pups.
claims.source: Analyses of postnatal bone development of Piezo1/2 mutant pups were performed by Masson's Trichrome staining, which showed reduction of collagens in the trabecular and cortical bones of the P5 Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant pups (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: Supported by Masson's Trichrome staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: Serum PINP levels are reduced in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mice.
claims.source: Bone formation was definitively examined by ELISA assays of serum procollagen type I N propeptide (PINP) levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c), which is considered clinically as the most sensitive bone formation marker (Samoszuk et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claims.claim: Mineralization apposition rate (MAR) and bone formation rate (BFR) are reduced in periosteum of cortical bone in Piezo1 CKO mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, histomorphometric analysis showed reduced mineralization apposition rate (MAR), and bone formation rate (BFR) in periosteum of the cortical bone of the Piezo1 CKO mice (Figure 2e, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by histomorphometric analysis data shown in Figure 2e.

claims.claim: Cortical bone formation in Piezo1/2 DKO mice is too severely reduced to allow accurate quantification.
claims.source: Reduction of cortical bone formation in the Piezo1/2 DKO mutant mice or trabecular bone formation in both Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mice were too severe to allow accurate quantification (Figure 2e,f).
claims.evidence: Supported by histomorphometric analysis data shown in Figure 2e,f.

claims.claim: Trabecular bone formation in both Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mice is too severely reduced to allow accurate quantification.
claims.source: Reduction of cortical bone formation in the Piezo1/2 DKO mutant mice or trabecular bone formation in both Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mice were too severe to allow accurate quantification (Figure 2e,f).
claims.evidence: Supported by histomorphometric analysis data shown in Figure 2e,f.

claims.claim: The secondary spongiosa is almost completely missing in Piezo1/2 DKO mice.
claims.source: In the Piezo1/2 DKO mice, the secondary spongiosa was almost completely missing.
claims.evidence: Inferred from histomorphometric analysis data.

claims.claim: Osteoclast marker expression (Ctsk and Acp5) is upregulated in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant mice.
claims.source: Reduction of bone formation in the Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant mice was accompanied by increase in bone remodeling indicated by upregulated expression of osteoclast markers Cathepsin K (Ctsk) and Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (Acp5 or Trap) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e,f).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e,f.

claims.claim: At E16.5, there is no difference in osteoclast marker expression between wild-type and Piezo1/2 mutants.
claims.source: However, earlier in development at E16.5, there was no difference in osteoclast marker expression (data not shown) suggesting that increased osteoclast differentiation may have resulted from the changes in osteoblast cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by unpublished data mentioned in the text.

claims.claim: Early and mature osteoblast marker expression is reduced in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at P0.
claims.source: Indeed, quantitative gene expression analysis by qRT-PCR further showed that while early and mature osteoblast marker expression were reduced, Tnfsf11 (Rankl) and Acp5 expression, indicative of osteoclast differentiation, were increased in the Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant at P0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g).
claims.evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1g.

claims.claim: Tnfsf11 (Rankl) and Acp5 expression is increased in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at P0.
claims.source: Indeed, quantitative gene expression analysis by qRT-PCR further showed that while early and mature osteoblast marker expression were reduced, Tnfsf11 (Rankl) and Acp5 expression, indicative of osteoclast differentiation, were increased in the Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant at P0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g).
claims.evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1g.

claims.claim: Tnfrsf11b (Opg) expression is reduced in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants.
claims.source: Expression of Tnfrsf11b (Opg), which encodes a decoy receptor of Tnfsf11 to inhibit osteoclast differentiation, was also reduced.
claims.evidence: Inferred from qRT-PCR data.

claims.claim: Reduced bone mass and density in the absence of Piezo channels is a combination of reduced bone formation and increased bone resorption.
claims.source: Therefore, reduced bone mass and density in the absence of Piezo channels is a combination of reduced bone formation and increased bone resorption, which resulted in not only bone fractures, but also reduced longitudinal bone growth and bone deformity such as bowing of the tibia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental data including μCT, histomorphometry, and gene expression analyses.

claims.claim: Expression of Sox9 and Col10a1 is similar in wild-type, Piezo1 CKO, and Piezo1/2 DKO embryos at E16.5 and P0.
claims.source: At E16.5 and P0, expression of the chondrocyte marker Sox9 and hypertrophic chondrocyte marker Col10a1 was similar in the wild-type control, Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO embryos (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting cartilage formation and chondrocyte hypertrophy was not regulated by Piezo1/2 in development.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Cartilage formation and chondrocyte hypertrophy are not regulated by Piezo1/2 in development.
claims.source: At E16.5 and P0, expression of the chondrocyte marker Sox9 and hypertrophic chondrocyte marker Col10a1 was similar in the wild-type control, Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO embryos (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting cartilage formation and chondrocyte hypertrophy was not regulated by Piezo1/2 in development.
claims.evidence: Inferred from similar expression patterns of chondrocyte markers in wild-type and mutant embryos.

claims.claim: Expression of Sp7 is markedly reduced in Piezo1 CKO humerus at E16.5 and P0.
claims.source: However, expression of the early osteoblast marker Sp7 was markedly reduced at E16.5 and P0 in the ossifying regions of the developing Piezo1 CKO humerus and further reduced in the Piezo1/2 DKO humerus (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Piezo1/2 are required to promote osteoblast differentiation in development.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Expression of Sp7 is further reduced in Piezo1/2 DKO humerus at E16.5 and P0.
claims.source: However, expression of the early osteoblast marker Sp7 was markedly reduced at E16.5 and P0 in the ossifying regions of the developing Piezo1 CKO humerus and further reduced in the Piezo1/2 DKO humerus (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Piezo1/2 are required to promote osteoblast differentiation in development.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Piezo1/2 are required to promote osteoblast differentiation in development.
claims.source: However, expression of the early osteoblast marker Sp7 was markedly reduced at E16.5 and P0 in the ossifying regions of the developing Piezo1 CKO humerus and further reduced in the Piezo1/2 DKO humerus (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Piezo1/2 are required to promote osteoblast differentiation in development.
claims.evidence: Inferred from reduced Sp7 expression in Piezo1/2 mutants.

claims.claim: Bone mineralization is reduced in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at P0.
claims.source: Bone mineralization and osteoblast maturation as indicated by von Kossa staining and secreted phosphoprotein 1 (Spp1, also known as Opn) immunofluorescent staining were also reduced in the trabecular and cortical bone areas at P0 (Figure 3d,e).
claims.evidence: Supported by von Kossa staining and Spp1 immunostaining data shown in Figure 3d,e.

claims.claim: Osteoblast maturation is reduced in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at P0.
claims.source: Bone mineralization and osteoblast maturation as indicated by von Kossa staining and secreted phosphoprotein 1 (Spp1, also known as Opn) immunofluorescent staining were also reduced in the trabecular and cortical bone areas at P0 (Figure 3d,e).
claims.evidence: Supported by von Kossa staining and Spp1 immunostaining data shown in Figure 3d,e.

claims.claim: Growth plate chondrocyte proliferation is reduced in Piezo1 CKO and further reduced in Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at E16.5.
claims.source: When examined by BrdU labeling, we found that growth plate chondrocyte proliferation and the length of the proliferative regions were both reduced in the Piezo1 CKO and further reduced in the Piezo1/2 DKO mutant at E16.5 (Figure 3b, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: The length of proliferative regions is reduced in Piezo1 CKO and further reduced in Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at E16.5.
claims.source: When examined by BrdU labeling, we found that growth plate chondrocyte proliferation and the length of the proliferative regions were both reduced in the Piezo1 CKO and further reduced in the Piezo1/2 DKO mutant at E16.5 (Figure 3b, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: Increased apoptosis is found in the bone and muscle of Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at E16.5.
claims.source: Increased apoptosis was found in the bone and muscle of the Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant at E16.5 by TUNEL assay (Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: Piezo1/2 MS channels are required for cartilage growth and bone formation in embryonic development.
claims.source: These analyses indicate that Piezo1/2 MS channels are required for cartilage growth and bone formation in embryonic development, providing mechanistic insights into findings made in human populations that PIEZO1 SNPs are associated with reduced body height and eBMD (Marouli et al., 2017; Morris et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental data and supported by human GWAS studies.

claims.claim: PIEZO1 SNPs are associated with reduced body height in humans.
claims.source: These analyses indicate that Piezo1/2 MS channels are required for cartilage growth and bone formation in embryonic development, providing mechanistic insights into findings made in human populations that PIEZO1 SNPs are associated with reduced body height and eBMD (Marouli et al., 2017; Morris et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to human GWAS study.

claims.claim: PIEZO1 SNPs are associated with reduced eBMD in humans.
claims.source: These analyses indicate that Piezo1/2 MS channels are required for cartilage growth and bone formation in embryonic development, providing mechanistic insights into findings made in human populations that PIEZO1 SNPs are associated with reduced body height and eBMD (Marouli et al., 2017; Morris et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to human GWAS study.

claims.claim: Sp7-Cre; Piezo1f/f and Sp7-Cre; Piezo1f/f; Piezo2f/f mouse pups do not show limb bone fractures.
claims.source: Interestingly, the Sp7-Cre; Piezo1f/f (Piezo1CKO) and Sp7-Cre; Piezo1f/f; Piezo2f/f (Piezo1/2 DKO) mouse pups did not show limb bone fractures.
claims.evidence: Supported by skeletal analysis data.

claims.claim: Multiple bone fractures are found in the ribs at P21 in Sp7-Cre-driven Piezo1CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mice.
claims.source: However, multiple bone fractures were found in the ribs at P21 in the Piezo1CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mice, but not the Piezo2 CKO mice (Figure 4a).
claims.evidence: Supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: Loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 in Sp7+ cells leads to reduced trabecular and cortical bones.
claims.source: μCT analyses showed that loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 in Sp7+ cells led to reduced trabecular and cortical bones (Figure 4b, Supplementary file 1, Source data 1) and Sp7 expression (Figure 4c).
claims.evidence: Supported by μCT data shown in Figure 4b and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 in Sp7+ cells leads to reduced Sp7 expression.
claims.source: μCT analyses showed that loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 in Sp7+ cells led to reduced trabecular and cortical bones (Figure 4b, Supplementary file 1, Source data 1) and Sp7 expression (Figure 4c).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4c.

claims.claim: Reduction in bone mass is more severe in Prrx1-Cre-driven mutants compared to Sp7-Cre-driven mutants.
claims.source: Reduction in bone mass was more severe in the Prrx1-Cre-driven mutants compared to the Sp7-Cre-driven ones (Figure 2d and Supplementary file 1), suggesting that Piezo1/2 in Sp7- cells such as the muscle, tenocytes and chondrocytes may also promote to bone formation.
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of μCT data from different Cre drivers.

claims.claim: Piezo1/2 in Sp7- cells such as muscle, tenocytes, and chondrocytes may also promote bone formation.
claims.source: Reduction in bone mass was more severe in the Prrx1-Cre-driven mutants compared to the Sp7-Cre-driven ones (Figure 2d and Supplementary file 1), suggesting that Piezo1/2 in Sp7- cells such as the muscle, tenocytes and chondrocytes may also promote to bone formation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of phenotypes between different Cre-driven mutants.

claims.claim: Mechanical stress slightly increases Piezo1 expression in Prrx1 lineage cells but not Sp7 lineage cells.
claims.source: In addition, we found that when cultured under osteogenic conditions, mechanical stress slightly increased Piezo1 expression in the Prrx1 lineage cells, not the Sp7 lineage cells (Figure 4d).
claims.evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4d.

claims.claim: Yoda1 promotes bone formation and osteoblast differentiation in wild-type limbs but not Piezo1/2 DKO limbs in explant culture.
claims.source: However, Yoda1 promoted bone formation and osteoblast differentiation in the wild type, but not the Piezo1/2 DKO limbs (Figure 5a), suggesting that Piezo1 was functional in the explant culture.
claims.evidence: Supported by limb explant culture data shown in Figure 5a.

claims.claim: The drastic difference in bone formation between wild-type and Sp7-Cre; Piezo1/2 DKO limbs developed in utero is eliminated in explant culture.
claims.source: Importantly, the drastic difference in bone formation between the wild-type control and the Sp7-Cre; Piezo1/2 DKO limbs developed in utero was eliminated (compare Figure 5b with Figure 4a,c).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of limb explant culture data (Figure 5b) with in vivo data (Figure 4a,c).

claims.claim: BTX injection reduces bone mass in wild-type mice.
claims.source: While BTX injection reduced bone mass in the wild-type mice, in the Sp7-Cre-driven Piezo1/2 DKO mice, BTX injection did not cause significant bone loss, although the bone mass was lower compared to that of the wild-type controls (Figure 5c, Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by μCT data from BTX-induced muscle paralysis model shown in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: BTX injection does not cause significant bone loss in Sp7-Cre-driven Piezo1/2 DKO mice.
claims.source: While BTX injection reduced bone mass in the wild-type mice, in the Sp7-Cre-driven Piezo1/2 DKO mice, BTX injection did not cause significant bone loss, although the bone mass was lower compared to that of the wild-type controls (Figure 5c, Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by μCT data from BTX-induced muscle paralysis model shown in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: Piezo1/2 are required for embryonic bone development and adult bone mass maintenance by mechanical forces.
claims.source: Taken together, Piezo1/2 are required for embryonic bone development and adult bone mass maintenance by mechanical forces.
claims.evidence: Inferred from limb explant culture and BTX-induced muscle paralysis experiments.

claims.claim: Ctnnb1 and Yap1/Wwtr1 protein levels are reduced in bones of Prrx1-Cre-driven Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at P0.
claims.source: We found that Ctnnb1 and Yap1/Wwtr1 protein levels were both reduced in the bones of Prrx1-Cre-driven Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at P0 and more reduction was found in the Piezo 1/2 DKO bone samples (Figure 6a,b, Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 6a,b.

claims.claim: Expression of Ctgf/Cyr61 and Tcf7/Lef1 is down-regulated in Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant bones.
claims.source: In addition, by qRT-PCR analysis, we found that expression of transcriptional targets of both Yap1/Wwtr1 and Wnt/Ctnnb1 such as Ctgf (Ccn2)/Cyr61(Ccn1) and Tcf7/Lef1, respectively, were down-regulated in the Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutant bones (Figure 6c, Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6c.

claims.claim: Ccn2 expression is reduced in developing humerus at E16.5 by removing Piezo1/2.
claims.source: These results were further confirmed by in situ hybridization with a Ccn2 probe using the RNAscope technology (Figure 6d). Ccn2 expression was reduced in the developing humerus at E16.5 by removing Piezo1/2.
claims.evidence: Supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6d.

claims.claim: Piezo1/2 activities may promote osteoblast differentiation by upregulating both Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 activities.
claims.source: These results show that Piezo1/2 activities may promote osteoblast differentiation by upregulating both Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 activities.
claims.evidence: Inferred from reduced Ctnnb1 and Yap1 protein levels and target gene expression in Piezo1/2 mutants.

claims.claim: BMSCs express both Piezo1 and Piezo2, but Piezo1 expression is stronger.
claims.source: The stiff surface of regular tissue culture dishes supports osteoblast differentiation of BMSCs, which expressed both Piezo1/2, but Piezo1 expression was stronger (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: Loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 in BMSCs leads to reduced osteoblast differentiation.
claims.source: However, loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 by Cre Adenovirus (Ad-Cre) infection of the Piezo1f/f or Piezo1f/f; Piezo2f/f BMSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), respectively, led to reduced osteoblast differentiation and reduced Yap1/Wwtr1 and Wnt/Ctnnb1 signaling activities (Figure 6e, Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 6e.

claims.claim: Loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 in BMSCs leads to reduced Yap1/Wwtr1 and Wnt/Ctnnb1 signaling activities.
claims.source: However, loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 by Cre Adenovirus (Ad-Cre) infection of the Piezo1f/f or Piezo1f/f; Piezo2f/f BMSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), respectively, led to reduced osteoblast differentiation and reduced Yap1/Wwtr1 and Wnt/Ctnnb1 signaling activities (Figure 6e, Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6e.

claims.claim: Treating wild-type BMSCs with Yoda1 increases osteoblast differentiation.
claims.source: Consistent with this, treating wild-type BMSCs with Yoda1 increased osteoblast differentiation as well as Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 transcriptional activities (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: Treating wild-type BMSCs with Yoda1 increases Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 transcriptional activities.
claims.source: Consistent with this, treating wild-type BMSCs with Yoda1 increased osteoblast differentiation as well as Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 transcriptional activities (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: The osteogenic activity of Yoda1 is lost in the absence of Piezo1/2.
claims.source: Such osteogenic activity of Yoda1 was lost in the absence of Piezo1/2 (Figure 6f, Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting that Yoda1 activity in promoting osteoblast differentiation depends on Piezo1.
claims.evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 6f.

claims.claim: Yoda1 activity in promoting osteoblast differentiation depends on Piezo1.
claims.source: Such osteogenic activity of Yoda1 was lost in the absence of Piezo1/2 (Figure 6f, Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting that Yoda1 activity in promoting osteoblast differentiation depends on Piezo1.
claims.evidence: Inferred from loss of Yoda1 effect in Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs.

claims.claim: Blocking Ca2+ influx with Gd3+ blocks osteoblast differentiation similar to loss of Piezo1/2.
claims.source: In addition, blocking Ca2+ influx with Gadolinium (Gd3+), a potent blocker of Calcium channels including the Piezos (Coste et al., 2010), blocked osteoblast differentiation similar to loss of Piezo1/2 (Figure 6f).
claims.evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 6f, and citation to previous work on Gd3+ as a calcium channel blocker.

claims.claim: Piezo1/2 depend on Ca2+ influx and mediate mechanotransduction via Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 pathways in regulating osteoblast differentiation of BMSCs.
claims.source: These results suggest that Piezo1/2 depend on Ca2+ influx and mediate mechanotransduction via the Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 pathways in regulating osteoblast differentiation of BMSCs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing effects of Piezo1/2 loss, Yoda1 treatment, and Gd3+ treatment on osteoblast differentiation and signaling pathways.

claims.claim: Loss of Piezo1/2 completely abolishes the response of BMSCs to FSS in osteogenic assay.
claims.source: We found that FSS stimulated osteoblast differentiation of wild-type BMSCs while loss of Piezo1/2 completely abolished the response of BMSC to FSS in the osteogenic assay (Figure 7a, Figure 7—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining and qPCR data shown in Figure 7a.

claims.claim: FSS upregulates protein levels of Ctnnb1 and Yap1 in BMSCs.
claims.source: Importantly, FSS upregulated protein levels of Ctnnb1 and Yap1, while levels of phosphorylated Ctnnb1 and Yap1, which are cytoplasmic and destined for degradation, were reduced by FSS in BMSCs, indicating that FSS activated both Ctnnb1 and Yap1 activities (Figure 7b).
claims.evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7b.

claims.claim: FSS reduces levels of phosphorylated Ctnnb1 and Yap1 in BMSCs.
claims.source: Importantly, FSS upregulated protein levels of Ctnnb1 and Yap1, while levels of phosphorylated Ctnnb1 and Yap1, which are cytoplasmic and destined for degradation, were reduced by FSS in BMSCs, indicating that FSS activated both Ctnnb1 and Yap1 activities (Figure 7b).
claims.evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7b.

claims.claim: FSS activates both Ctnnb1 and Yap1 activities in BMSCs.
claims.source: Importantly, FSS upregulated protein levels of Ctnnb1 and Yap1, while levels of phosphorylated Ctnnb1 and Yap1, which are cytoplasmic and destined for degradation, were reduced by FSS in BMSCs, indicating that FSS activated both Ctnnb1 and Yap1 activities (Figure 7b).
claims.evidence: Inferred from increased total protein and decreased phosphorylated forms of Ctnnb1 and Yap1 upon FSS treatment.

claims.claim: Piezo1/2 loss in BMSCs abolishes osteogenic response to FSS.
claims.source: Piezo1/2 loss in BMSCs abolished osteogenic response to FSS, reduced Ctnnb1 and Yap1 protein levels and increased Ctnnb1 and Yap1 phosphorylation (Figure 7a,b).
claims.evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining, qPCR, and Western blot data shown in Figure 7a,b.

claims.claim: Piezo1/2 loss in BMSCs reduces Ctnnb1 and Yap1 protein levels.

claims.claim: Piezo1/2 channels in BMSCs sense FSS-like mechanical forces to allow Ca2+ influx, leading to osteoblast differentiation.

claims.claim: CsA treatment abolishes osteoblast differentiation enhanced by Yoda1 treatment.

claims.claim: Loss of Piezo1/2 together leads to a strong increase of Nfatc1 phosphorylation in developing bone.

claims.claim: Loss of Piezo1 alone increases Nfatc1 phosphorylation, although to a lesser extent than Piezo1/2 loss.

claims.claim: Piezo1/2 activate Nfatc1 by inhibiting its phosphorylation in developing bone.

claims.evidence: Inferred from increased Nfatc1 phosphorylation in Piezo1/2 mutants, supported by citations to previous work on NFAT regulation.

claims.claim: Yoda1 treatment stimulates transcription activities of NFAT, YAP1, and CTNNB1 in HEK293T cells.

claims.claim: Knocking down PIEZO1 abolishes Yoda1-stimulated transcription activities of NFAT, YAP1, and CTNNB1.

claims.claim: Activation of PIEZO1 upregulates NFATc1, YAP1, and CTNNB1 transcriptional activities.

claims.evidence: Inferred from luciferase reporter assay results showing Yoda1 effects.

claims.claim: Transcriptional activities of NFAT, YAP1, and CTNNB1 are mutually enhanced, with the exception that YAP1 does not enhance NFAT activities in HEK293T cells.

claims.claim: YAP1 and NFATc1 interaction is promoted by FSS or Yoda1 treatment.

claims.claim: YAP1 and NFATc1 interaction is inhibited by CsA or Gd3+ treatment.

claims.evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9c and Figure 9—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: PIEZO1-induced Ca2+ signaling promotes NFATc1 interaction with YAP1.

claims.claim: NFATc1 and YAP1 nuclear localization are both robustly promoted by FSS in HEK293 cells.

claims.claim: Overexpression of PPP3CA promotes YAP1 dephosphorylation.

claims.claim: Yoda1 treatment mimics the effects of FSS treatment or PPP3CA expression on YAP1 and NFATc1 nuclear localization.
claims.source: Moreover, Yoda1 treatment mimicked the effects of FSS treatment or PPP3CA expression (Figure 9e, Figure 9—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9e and Western blot data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: Gd3+ treatment inhibits nuclear localization of NFATc1 and YAP1 induced by FSS or Yoda1 treatment.

claims.claim: NFATc1 interaction with YAP1 or CTNNB1 is synergistically promoted by the presence of all three transcription factors.

claims.claim: Gd3+ treatment promotes Yap1 and Ctnnb1 phosphorylation while reducing their protein levels within 30 min.

claims.claim: Ppp3ca binds to Nfatc1, Yap1, and Ctnnb1 in mouse primary BMSCs.

claims.claim: Ppp3ca binding to Nfatc1, Yap1, and Ctnnb1 is enhanced by Yoda1 treatment.

claims.source: Mechanistically, Piezo1/2 relayed fluid shear stress and extracellular matrix stiffness signals to activate Ca2+ influx to stimulate Calcineurin, which promotes concerted activation of NFATc1, YAP1 and ß-catenin transcription factors by inducing their dephosphorylation as well as NFAT/YAP1/ß-catenin complex formation.
claims.evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing interactions between NFATc1, YAP1, and ß-catenin.

results.result: Piezo1 and Piezo2 are expressed in distinct but overlapping patterns during embryonic limb development. Piezo1 is predominantly expressed in the interdigit region, connective tissue, muscle, and differentiating osteoblasts in the perichondrium/periosteum, as well as in hypertrophic chondrocytes, tendons, and ligaments. Piezo2 is expressed in forming digits and wrist, with lineage tracing showing Piezo2+ cells include osteoblasts, joint cells, sporadic chondrocytes, tendons, and connective tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are well-supported by multiple complementary techniques including whole mount in situ hybridization (WISH), RNAscope, immunostaining with Piezo1-tdTomato reporter mice, and lineage tracing with Piezo2-EGFP-Cre crossed to Rosa-tdTomato. The expression patterns are documented across multiple developmental stages (E12.5-P0) with consistent results shown in Figures 1 and supplementary figures.

results.result: Loss of Piezo1 in mesenchymal progenitors (Prrx1-Cre) causes multiple bone fractures in radius and ulna at birth, while Piezo2 loss alone shows normal skeletal development. Piezo1/2 double knockout (DKO) mice exhibit more severe defects with additional femur fractures. Long bones are shortened in Piezo1 mutants but not Piezo2 mutants, with further shortening in DKO mice, indicating Piezo1 plays a major role while Piezo2 has redundant functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C13 are strongly supported by skeletal staining and μCT analyses shown in Figure 2a,b. The graded severity of phenotypes (Piezo2 CKO < Piezo1 CKO < Piezo1/2 DKO) provides clear evidence for the relative contributions and redundancy of the two channels. Quantitative measurements of bone length support the conclusions about differential roles.

results.result: Piezo1 expression progressively increases postnatally in young mice, while Piezo2 mRNA expression is reduced in postnatal cortical bone.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15 are supported by Western blotting and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b. The differential postnatal expression patterns suggest distinct temporal roles for the two channels, with Piezo1 becoming more important postnatally when mechanical stress increases.

results.result: At P21, both cortical and trabecular bone masses are reduced in Piezo1 CKO mice and further reduced in Piezo1/2 DKO mice, while Piezo2 CKO mice exhibit normal bone mass.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 are well-supported by μCT analyses shown in Figure 2c,d with quantitative data. The consistent pattern of Piezo2 CKO showing no defect while Piezo1 CKO and especially Piezo1/2 DKO show progressive defects reinforces the conclusion about relative importance and redundancy.

results.result: Bone formation is severely impaired in Piezo1 and Piezo1/2 mutants, as evidenced by reduced collagen content (Masson's Trichrome), reduced serum PINP levels, and reduced mineralization apposition rate (MAR) and bone formation rate (BFR). The defects are so severe in Piezo1/2 DKO mice that trabecular bone formation and cortical bone formation cannot be accurately quantified, with the secondary spongiosa almost completely missing.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 are supported by multiple complementary assays including histological staining, ELISA for serum PINP (a clinically validated bone formation marker), and histomorphometric analysis with calcein labeling shown in Figure 2e,f and supplementary figures. The inability to quantify bone formation in the most severe mutants is appropriately acknowledged and itself indicates the severity of the phenotype.

results.result: Reduced bone formation in Piezo1/2 mutants is accompanied by increased bone resorption, indicated by upregulated osteoclast markers (Ctsk, Acp5/Trap) and increased Tnfsf11 (Rankl) expression with reduced Tnfrsf11b (Opg) expression at P0. However, at E16.5, osteoclast marker expression is unchanged, suggesting increased osteoclast differentiation is secondary to osteoblast defects. The combined reduction in bone formation and increase in bone resorption results in bone fractures, reduced longitudinal growth, and bone deformities.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C30 are supported by immunostaining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e,f) and qRT-PCR data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g). The temporal analysis showing normal osteoclast markers at E16.5 but increased expression later provides important mechanistic insight that the osteoclast phenotype is likely secondary to the primary osteoblast defect. The inference about combined effects is logical given the data.

results.result: Cartilage formation and chondrocyte hypertrophy are not regulated by Piezo1/2 in development, as Sox9 and Col10a1 expression are similar in wild-type and mutant embryos at E16.5 and P0. However, expression of the early osteoblast marker Sp7 is markedly reduced in Piezo1 CKO and further reduced in Piezo1/2 DKO humerus, indicating Piezo1/2 are required to promote osteoblast differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 are supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a and supplementary figures. The differential effects on chondrocyte markers (unchanged) versus osteoblast markers (reduced) provide clear evidence that Piezo1/2 specifically regulate osteoblast differentiation rather than having general effects on skeletal development.

results.result: Bone mineralization and osteoblast maturation are reduced in Piezo1/2 mutants at P0 (von Kossa and Spp1 staining). Growth plate chondrocyte proliferation and proliferative region length are reduced in Piezo1 CKO and further reduced in Piezo1/2 DKO at E16.5 (BrdU labeling). Increased apoptosis is found in bone and muscle of mutants at E16.5 (TUNEL assay).
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 are supported by appropriate histological and immunostaining methods shown in Figure 3b-e. The BrdU labeling provides quantitative data on proliferation, and the TUNEL assay appropriately identifies apoptosis. These findings extend the characterization of the skeletal phenotype beyond just bone formation to include effects on chondrocyte proliferation and cell survival.

results.result: Piezo1/2 mechanosensitive channels are required for cartilage growth and bone formation in embryonic development, providing mechanistic insights into human GWAS findings that PIEZO1 SNPs are associated with reduced body height and estimated bone mineral density (eBMD).
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 are supported by the cumulative experimental evidence from the mouse studies and appropriately cite human GWAS studies (Marouli et al., 2017; Morris et al., 2019). The connection between mouse genetics and human genetics is reasonable, though the claim about providing "mechanistic insights" is somewhat overstated since the specific SNPs and their functional consequences are not directly tested. The human GWAS associations are cited but not independently verified in this study.

results.result: Using Sp7-Cre to delete Piezo1/2 in osteoblast progenitors, Piezo1CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mouse pups do not show limb bone fractures at birth but develop multiple rib fractures by P21. Loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 in Sp7+ cells leads to reduced trabecular and cortical bones and reduced Sp7 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are supported by skeletal staining and μCT analyses shown in Figure 4a-c. The differential timing of fractures (ribs at P21 but not limbs at birth) compared to Prrx1-Cre mutants provides important information about the cell-type specificity and timing of Piezo1/2 function. The μCT quantification and Sp7 immunostaining provide robust support.

results.result: Bone mass reduction is more severe in Prrx1-Cre-driven mutants compared to Sp7-Cre-driven mutants, suggesting Piezo1/2 in Sp7-negative cells (muscle, tenocytes, chondrocytes) may also promote bone formation. Mechanical stress slightly increases Piezo1 expression in Prrx1 lineage cells but not Sp7 lineage cells under osteogenic culture conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are supported by comparison of μCT data between different Cre drivers (Figure 2d, Figure 4b, Supplementary file 1) and RT-qPCR data (Figure 4d). The inference about contributions from Sp7-negative cells is reasonable given the differential severity. However, the claim about mechanical stress effects on Piezo1 expression (C50) shows only "slight" increases and may have limited biological significance.

results.result: In limb explant culture under static conditions (reduced mechanical forces), Yoda1 (Piezo1 agonist) promotes bone formation and osteoblast differentiation in wild-type but not Piezo1/2 DKO limbs. Importantly, the drastic difference in bone formation between wild-type and Sp7-Cre; Piezo1/2 DKO limbs observed in utero is eliminated in explant culture.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 are supported by limb explant culture data shown in Figure 5a,b. The elimination of the phenotypic difference in explant culture (reduced mechanical loading) compared to in vivo development provides strong evidence that Piezo1/2 function depends on mechanical forces. The Yoda1 specificity (works in WT but not DKO) confirms on-target effects.

results.result: In a botulinum toxin (BTX)-induced muscle paralysis model of unloading, BTX injection reduces bone mass in wild-type mice but does not cause significant bone loss in Sp7-Cre-driven Piezo1/2 DKO mice (though baseline bone mass is lower). Together, these results indicate Piezo1/2 are required for embryonic bone development and adult bone mass maintenance by mechanical forces.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by μCT data from the BTX model shown in Figure 5c. The resistance of Piezo1/2 DKO mice to further bone loss upon unloading provides strong evidence that Piezo1/2 mediate mechanical force effects on bone. However, the interpretation is complicated by the already reduced baseline bone mass in mutants, which could create a "floor effect." The statistical analysis appears appropriate (paired comparisons).

results.result: Ctnnb1 and Yap1/Wwtr1 protein levels are reduced in bones of Piezo1 CKO and Piezo1/2 DKO mutants at P0, with greater reduction in DKO. Expression of transcriptional targets of Yap1/Wwtr1 (Ctgf/Cyr61) and Wnt/Ctnnb1 (Tcf7/Lef1) are down-regulated in mutant bones, confirmed by RNAscope for Ccn2. These results suggest Piezo1/2 activities promote osteoblast differentiation by upregulating both Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 activities.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 are supported by immunostaining, Western blot, qRT-PCR, and RNAscope data shown in Figure 6a-d. The convergence of multiple methods and the examination of both the transcription factors themselves and their downstream targets provide strong support. The inference about mechanism (C59) is reasonable but somewhat speculative since direct causation is not established.

results.result: Bone marrow stromal cells (BMSCs) express both Piezo1 and Piezo2, with stronger Piezo1 expression. Loss of Piezo1 or Piezo1/2 by Ad-Cre infection leads to reduced osteoblast differentiation and reduced Yap1/Wwtr1 and Wnt/Ctnnb1 signaling activities in BMSCs cultured on stiff surfaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are supported by Western blot data showing Piezo1/2 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a) and alkaline phosphatase staining plus qPCR data showing reduced osteoblast differentiation and signaling (Figure 6e). The use of Ad-Cre for acute deletion in cultured cells is appropriate and avoids developmental compensation.

results.result: Treating wild-type BMSCs with Yoda1 (Piezo1 agonist) increases osteoblast differentiation and Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 transcriptional activities. The osteogenic activity of Yoda1 is lost in the absence of Piezo1/2, indicating Yoda1 activity in promoting osteoblast differentiation depends on Piezo1.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 are supported by luciferase reporter assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b) and alkaline phosphatase staining/qPCR (Figure 6f). The loss of Yoda1 effect in Piezo1/2-deficient cells confirms specificity and on-target activity. This provides important pharmacological validation of the genetic findings.

results.result: Blocking Ca2+ influx with Gadolinium (Gd3+), a calcium channel blocker including Piezos, blocks osteoblast differentiation similar to loss of Piezo1/2. These results suggest Piezo1/2 depend on Ca2+ influx and mediate mechanotransduction via Wnt/Ctnnb1 and Yap1 pathways in regulating osteoblast differentiation of BMSCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are supported by alkaline phosphatase staining and qPCR data (Figure 6f) and cite previous work on Gd3+ as a calcium channel blocker (Coste et al., 2010). However, Gd3+ is not specific to Piezo channels and blocks multiple calcium channels, so the interpretation that effects are specifically through Piezo channels is somewhat uncertain. The inference about Ca2+-dependence is reasonable but not definitively proven.

results.result: Fluid shear stress (FSS) stimulates osteoblast differentiation of wild-type BMSCs, while loss of Piezo1/2 completely abolishes the response to FSS. FSS upregulates total Ctnnb1 and Yap1 protein levels while reducing their phosphorylated (inactive) forms, indicating activation of both pathways. Piezo1/2 loss abolishes these FSS-induced changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C75 are supported by alkaline phosphatase staining, qPCR, and Western blot data shown in Figure 7a,b. The FSS system using a rocking platform is a well-established method. The complete abolishment of FSS response in Piezo1/2-deficient cells provides strong evidence for their role as mechanosensors. The Western blot data showing changes in both total and phosphorylated forms of Ctnnb1 and Yap1 provide mechanistic insight.

results.result: FSS-stimulated Yap1 activation may be independent of the canonical Hippo pathway (Stk3/4 and Lats kinase cascade), as increased Yap1 phosphorylation in Piezo1/2 mutants is not accompanied by increased phosphorylation of Stk4 (Mst1) or Lats1. These results suggest Piezo1/2 are key mechanical force sensors that relay FSS signals to promote osteoblast differentiation through Yap1 and Ctnnb1 signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 are supported by Western blot data (Figure 7b) showing no change in phospho-Stk4 or phospho-Lats1 despite changes in phospho-Yap1. This suggests a non-canonical mechanism of Yap1 regulation, which is an important mechanistic insight. However, the lack of change in upstream kinases doesn't definitively prove independence from the Hippo pathway, as other regulatory mechanisms could be involved. The overall conclusion (C77) is well-supported by the cumulative evidence.

results.result: Using GCaMP5G calcium indicator, basal Ca2+ signal is stronger in wild-type BMSCs compared to Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs. FSS induces more robust Ca2+ influx in wild-type BMSCs compared to Piezo-deficient cells. Yoda1 treatment leads to more robust Ca2+ influx in wild-type but not Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs. These results indicate Piezo1/2 channels in BMSCs sense FSS-like mechanical forces to allow Ca2+ influx, leading to osteoblast differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 are supported by calcium imaging data using the GCaMP5G reporter shown in Figure 7c, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, and Videos 1-2. The use of a genetically encoded calcium indicator provides direct evidence for Piezo1/2-dependent calcium signaling. The differential responses to FSS and Yoda1 between wild-type and mutant cells provide strong support for the mechanistic model.

results.result: Wild-type BMSCs show matrix stiffness-dependent behavior: difficulty spreading with diffused Yap1 localization on soft matrix (1 kPa), but spreading to larger areas with strong nuclear Yap1 localization on stiff matrix (40 kPa). Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs on stiff matrix behave like wild-type BMSCs on soft matrix, showing weaker Ca2+ signaling, less spreading, less defined Yap1 nuclear localization, and reduced Yap1 activities and osteoblast differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C88 are supported by immunostaining on hydrogels (Figure 8a), calcium imaging (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), and alkaline phosphatase staining/qPCR (Figure 8b). The hydrogel system with defined stiffness is well-established for studying mechanotransduction. The finding that Piezo1/2-deficient cells cannot properly sense matrix stiffness provides important evidence for their role as mechanosensors beyond just FSS.

results.result: Piezo1/2 promote osteoblast differentiation by sensing matrix stiffness that regulates Yap1 nuclear localization.
results.evaluation: Claim C89 is supported by the hydrogel experiments (C82-C88) showing that Piezo1/2-deficient cells fail to properly respond to matrix stiffness. The connection to Yap1 nuclear localization is well-documented in the literature and confirmed by the immunostaining data. This represents an important extension of Piezo1/2 function beyond FSS to include matrix stiffness sensing.

results.result: Cyclosporin A (CsA), a calcineurin (Ppp3ca) inhibitor, abolishes osteoblast differentiation and Yap1/Ctnnb1 activation enhanced by FSS or Yoda1 treatment. These results suggest Ppp3ca acts downstream of Piezo1/2 in mechanotransduction to regulate Yap1 and Ctnnb1 activities during osteoblast differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C94 are supported by alkaline phosphatase staining, qPCR, and luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 8c,d and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b. The use of CsA, a well-characterized calcineurin inhibitor, provides pharmacological evidence for the role of calcineurin in the pathway. The inference that Ppp3ca acts downstream is reasonable given that CsA blocks the effects of both FSS and Yoda1.

results.result: Loss of Piezo1/2 together leads to strong increase in Nfatc1 phosphorylation in developing bone, with loss of Piezo1 alone also increasing phosphorylation to a lesser extent. Since Nfat transcription factors are dephosphorylated by Ppp3ca upon Ca2+ influx, leading to nuclear translocation and gene activation, these results suggest Piezo1/2 activate Nfatc1 by inhibiting its phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are supported by Western blot data showing increased phospho-Nfatc1 in mutants (Figure 9a) and cite established literature on NFAT regulation by calcineurin (Liu et al., 1997; Masuda et al., 1997; Beals et al., 1997; Crabtree and Olson, 2002). The inference about mechanism is reasonable given the well-established role of calcineurin in NFAT dephosphorylation. This extends the mechanistic understanding to include NFAT as a third transcription factor in the pathway.

results.result: In HEK293T cells, Yoda1 treatment stimulates transcription activities of NFAT, YAP1, and CTNNB1, all of which are abolished by PIEZO1 knockdown. Transcriptional activities of NFAT, YAP1, and CTNNB1 are mutually enhanced, with the exception that YAP1 does not enhance NFAT activities in HEK293T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C101 are supported by luciferase reporter assays in HEK293T cells shown in Figure 9b and Figure 9—figure supplement 1b. The use of siRNA knockdown confirms specificity of Yoda1 effects. The mutual enhancement of transcription factors suggests complex crosstalk, though the exception for YAP1 not enhancing NFAT is noted. The use of HEK293T cells (not bone cells) is a limitation but provides proof-of-principle.

results.result: YAP1 and NFATc1 interaction is promoted by FSS or Yoda1 treatment but inhibited by CsA or Gd3+ treatment, as shown by co-immunoprecipitation. These results suggest PIEZO1-induced Ca2+ signaling promotes NFATc1 interaction with YAP1.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9c and Figure 9—figure supplement 1b. The demonstration of physical interaction between NFATc1 and YAP1 that is regulated by Piezo1 activity provides important mechanistic insight into how these pathways converge. The effects of CsA and Gd3+ support the role of Ca2+/calcineurin signaling.

results.result: In HEK293 cells, both NFATc1 and YAP1 nuclear localization are robustly promoted by FSS. Overexpression of PPP3CA (calcineurin catalytic subunit) promotes YAP1 dephosphorylation. Yoda1 treatment mimics the effects of FSS or PPP3CA expression. Blocking Ca2+ influx with Gd3+ or PPP3CA activity with CsA inhibits nuclear localization of NFATc1 and YAP1 induced by FSS or Yoda1.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 9d,e) and Western blot data (Figure 9—figure supplement 1c). The convergence of multiple approaches (FSS, Yoda1, PPP3CA overexpression, CsA, Gd3+) provides strong support for the model that Piezo1-induced Ca2+ signaling activates calcineurin, which then promotes nuclear localization of both NFATc1 and YAP1 through dephosphorylation.

results.result: NFATc1 interaction with YAP1 or CTNNB1 is synergistically promoted when all three transcription factors are present together, as shown by co-immunoprecipitation.
results.evaluation: Claim C110 is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1d. The demonstration of synergistic complex formation suggests cooperative binding and provides mechanistic insight into how these three pathways converge to regulate transcription. This is an important finding for understanding the integration of multiple signaling pathways.

results.result: In mouse primary BMSCs, Yoda1 treatment quickly reduces Yap1 and Ctnnb1 phosphorylation, an effect abolished in Piezo1/2-deficient BMSCs. Conversely, blocking Ca2+ influx with Gd3+ promotes Yap1 and Ctnnb1 phosphorylation while reducing their protein levels within 30 minutes.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 are supported by Western blot data showing rapid changes in phosphorylation status (Figure 9f, Figure 9—figure supplement 1e,f). The rapid kinetics (within 30 min) and the opposite effects of Yoda1 versus Gd3+ provide strong evidence for direct regulation of Yap1 and Ctnnb1 phosphorylation by Piezo1/2-mediated Ca2+ signaling. The use of primary BMSCs (not cell lines) strengthens the findings.

results.result: In mouse primary BMSCs, Ppp3ca (calcineurin) binds to Nfatc1, Yap1, and Ctnnb1. These interactions are enhanced by Yoda1 treatment and inhibited by CsA.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C116 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from primary BMSCs shown in Figure 9g. The demonstration that calcineurin physically interacts with all three transcription factors (not just NFAT) is a novel and important finding. The regulation of these interactions by Yoda1 and CsA provides strong support for the model that calcineurin directly dephosphorylates all three transcription factors.

results.result: Ca2+/Ppp3ca signaling activated by Piezo1 leads to concerted activation of Yap1 and Ctnnb1 with Nfat, all of which act together to regulate transcription changes that promote osteoblast differentiation and bone formation.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 represents the overall mechanistic model and is supported by the cumulative evidence from claims C95-C116. The model integrating Piezo1/2 → Ca2+ → calcineurin → dephosphorylation of NFATc1/YAP1/CTNNB1 → complex formation → transcriptional activation is well-supported by multiple complementary approaches including genetics, pharmacology, biochemistry, and cell biology. This is a major conceptual advance in understanding mechanotransduction in bone.

results.result: BIO treatment (GSK3 inhibitor to activate Wnt/Ctnnb1 signaling) increases long bone length, bone mass, and reduces bone fractures in Piezo1/2 DKO mice. BIO treatment enhances Sp7 and Spp1 expression while reducing Ctsk expression, indicating increased Ctnnb1 activities enhance osteoblast differentiation and maturation while inhibiting osteoclast differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C122 are supported by skeletal staining, μCT, and immunostaining data shown in Figure 10a,b and supplementary figures. The partial rescue of the Piezo1/2 mutant phenotype by activating Wnt/Ctnnb1 signaling provides important validation that reduced Ctnnb1 activity contributes to the bone defects. However, the rescue is only partial, consistent with the model that multiple pathways (NFAT, YAP1, CTNNB1) need to be activated.

results.result: In BMSCs, BIO treatment increases Ctnnb1 protein levels and reduces Ctnnb1 phosphorylation, and also increases Yap1 protein levels and reduces Yap1 phosphorylation. XMU-MP-1 (Hippo kinase inhibitor) treatment reduces Yap1 phosphorylation and increases Ctnnb1 levels. Verteporfin (Yap1 inhibitor) reduces BIO's effects on both Ctnnb1 and Yap1 levels, suggesting Ctnnb1 requires Yap1 activity to be fully upregulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127 are supported by Western blot data (Figure 10—figure supplement 1c) and cite appropriate literature for the inhibitors used. The demonstration of mutual regulation between Ctnnb1 and Yap1 pathways provides important mechanistic insight. However, the interpretation that "Ctnnb1 requires Yap1 activity to be fully upregulated" (C127) is somewhat strong given that the data show reduction but not complete elimination of BIO's effects by Verteporfin.

results.result: BIO treatment partially rescues reduction of osteoblast differentiation due to Piezo1/2 loss in BMSCs in vitro. In vivo, BIO treatment increases Ctnnb1 protein levels but the increase in Yap1 is less appreciable in Piezo1/2 mutant bones. This suggests that while Ctnnb1 activation is essential for osteoblast differentiation and can promote Yap1 activation, Yap1 is also regulated by Piezo1/2 through Ctnnb1-independent pathways, and concerted activation of NFATc1, Yap1, and Ctnnb1 constitutes a fully functional mechanotransduction pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C132 are supported by alkaline phosphatase staining/qPCR data (Figure 10—figure supplement 1d) and immunostaining data (Figure 10c). The partial rescue by BIO and the differential effects on Ctnnb1 versus Yap1 provide important evidence for the model that multiple pathways need to be activated for full mechanotransduction. The conclusion about concerted activation (C132) is well-supported by the cumulative evidence, though it remains somewhat inferential.

results.result: In a preliminary study of human BMSCs from 11 male subjects, PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 expression shows a significant negative correlation with age, suggesting reduction of PIEZO channels might contribute to bone aging.
results.evaluation: Claim C133 is supported by qRT-PCR data from human BMSCs shown in Figure 11, with PIEZO1 showing significant correlation (R=-0.6182, P=0.05) and PIEZO2 showing a trend (R=-0.5364, P=0.1). However, the sample size is small (n=11), only males are included, and the correlation for PIEZO2 is not statistically significant. The inference about contribution to bone aging (C134) is speculative and not directly tested. This is explicitly described as a "preliminary study" by the authors, which is appropriate. Additional studies with larger sample sizes, both sexes, and functional validation would be needed to support this conclusion.

results.result: Summary of major findings: Piezo1 and Piezo2 are mechanosensitive channels required for bone development and osteoblast differentiation. Loss of Piezo1 (or more severely Piezo1/2) in mesenchymal or osteoblast progenitor cells leads to multiple spontaneous bone fractures in newborn mice due to inhibition of osteoblast differentiation and increased bone resorption. Loss of Piezo1/2 renders mice resistant to further bone loss caused by unloading in both bone development and homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C138 represent summary statements of the major findings and are well-supported by the cumulative evidence from the entire study. These claims accurately reflect the key conclusions from the genetic, cellular, and molecular analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Mechanistic summary: Piezo1/2 relay fluid shear stress and extracellular matrix stiffness signals to activate Ca2+ influx, which stimulates Calcineurin (Ppp3ca). Calcineurin promotes concerted activation of NFATc1, YAP1, and β-catenin transcription factors by inducing their dephosphorylation and promoting NFAT/YAP1/β-catenin complex formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C142 represent the overall mechanistic model and are well-supported by the extensive biochemical, cellular, and molecular data presented throughout the study. The model is supported by multiple complementary approaches including genetics, pharmacology, co-immunoprecipitation, calcium imaging, and transcriptional reporter assays. This represents a major conceptual advance in understanding mechanotransduction.

results.result: Yap1 and β-catenin activities are reduced in Piezo1 and Piezo1/2 mutant bones, and these defects are partially rescued by enhanced β-catenin activities (BIO treatment).
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C144 are supported by immunostaining, Western blot, qPCR data, and the BIO rescue experiments. The partial rescue validates that reduced Ctnnb1 activity contributes to the phenotype while also supporting the model that multiple pathways need to be activated for full function.
